questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has 2 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when she breathes in or lies back and eases when she leans forward. She had a cold last week. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Widespread concave ST elevation with ST depression in aVR: not one coronary territory.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Positional pleuritic pain eased by leaning forward after a viral illness, with widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation not confined to one territory, is acute pericarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: worse when she breathes in or lies back
She had a cold last week
steps.x: **Positional** pain eased sitting forward after a **viral** illness, and ST elevation in **every territory** = pericarditis.

elim: A STEMI gives ST elevation in one coronary territory with reciprocal depression, and pain not eased by leaning forward.
Dissection gives tearing pain to the back with BP differences.
PE gives pleuritic pain with hypoxia and tachycardia; it does not ease sitting forward.
Takotsubo follows emotional stress and mimics an anterior MI.

steps.x: **B. Acute pericarditis.** Widespread saddle ST elevation + positional pain = acute pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has 3 days of fever, myalgia and sharp central chest pain that is worse on coughing and better sitting forward. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. His chest is clear. He is examined with the stethoscope at the left sternal edge while leaning forward.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
questions.e: A scratchy pericardial friction rub, best heard at the left sternal edge leaning forward, is the classic sign of acute pericarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: worse on coughing and better sitting forward
steps.x: Flu-like illness + positional pain = pericarditis; the sign is the **friction rub**.

elim: An early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation.
An ejection systolic murmur is aortic stenosis or flow.
An opening snap is mitral stenosis.
A third heart sound suggests heart failure.

steps.x: **D. Pericardial friction rub.** Acute pericarditis: scratchy friction rub, best leaning forward.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student has acute pericarditis confirmed on ECG. Ten days ago he had a sore throat, runny nose and a vesicular rash on his hands and in his mouth; his flatmate, a nursery worker, had the same illness. He has no past medical history and does not take drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pericarditis?
questions.e: Viral infection is the most important cause of acute pericarditis; hand, foot and mouth features point to Coxsackie virus.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: vesicular rash on his hands and in his mouth
steps.x: A preceding **viral** illness with hand and mouth vesicles = **Coxsackie**, a classic viral cause.

elim: Behçet's gives recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and arthritis.
Dressler's occurs weeks after an MI.
Streptococcal infection causes rheumatic fever, not hand and mouth vesicles.
He has no kidney disease.

steps.x: **B. Coxsackie virus infection.** Commonest cause of pericarditis: viral (Coxsackie, EBV, CMV, HIV, echovirus, VZV).

questions.stem: A 32 year old man of Turkish origin has acute pericarditis. He has had recurrent painful mouth ulcers for 3 years, two episodes of painful genital ulcers and a red, painful eye last year. A pustule formed where blood was taken last week. His temperature is 37.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his pericarditis?
questions.e: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and pathergy in a man from the Silk Road region suggest Behçet's syndrome, a recognised cause of acute pericarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: pustule formed where blood was taken
steps.x: Oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + **pathergy** = **Behçet's**.

elim: A viral cause would not explain years of oral and genital ulcers.
Reactive arthritis gives urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis after infection, not pathergy.
SLE ulcers are usually painless and genital ulcers are not typical.
TB causes chronic constrictive disease with weight loss and sweats.

steps.x: **A. Behçet's syndrome.** Pericarditis + oral/genital ulcers + uveitis: Behçet's.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with stage 5 chronic kidney disease has missed dialysis sessions for 2 weeks. He has central chest pain eased by sitting forward. There is a pericardial friction rub. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pericarditis?
questions.e: Uraemic pericarditis occurs in advanced CKD with a high urea, especially when dialysis is missed.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
CKD + missed dialysis + very high urea + rub = **uraemic** pericarditis.

elim: No viral prodrome is described; the urea explains it.
Dressler's follows a myocardial infarction.
High potassium causes ECG changes and arrhythmias, not pericarditis.
There are no features of SLE.

steps.x: **E. Uraemia.** Pericarditis in CKD with high urea = uraemic pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with known non-Hodgkin lymphoma has 4 weeks of increasing breathlessness and dull chest discomfort. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg and no pulsus paradoxus. His JVP is raised at 6 cm and heart sounds are quiet. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with clear lungs: the water bottle sign.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Malignancy with progressive breathlessness, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and a globular water-bottle heart is a pericardial effusion; normal BP and no pulsus paradoxus argue against tamponade.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Malignancy + **muffled** heart sounds + **water bottle** heart = effusion. BP is normal, so not (yet) tamponade.

elim: Tamponade needs hypotension and usually pulsus paradoxus; his BP is normal.
Heart failure gives cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema and loud, not muffled, sounds.
Constriction gives a small or normal heart, often with calcification.
SVC obstruction gives facial swelling and a non-pulsatile raised JVP, not a globular heart.

steps.x: **D. Pericardial effusion.** Muffled sounds + raised JVP + water bottle heart, BP normal = pericardial effusion.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation becomes dizzy and breathless over 6 hours. Her INR is 7.4. Her pulse rate is 126 bpm, BP 80/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her neck veins are distended and heart sounds are very quiet. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Spontaneous bleeding on over-anticoagulation is a risk factor for tamponade; hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds are Beck's triad, confirmed on echocardiography.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
**Beck's triad**: hypotension + raised JVP + muffled sounds, with **over-anticoagulation** as the cause of bleeding.

elim: MI cardiogenic shock gives chest pain and crackles, with normal heart sounds.
Massive PE gives hypoxia and a raised JVP but not muffled sounds; she is on warfarin.
Retroperitoneal bleeding causes hypotension with a low, not raised, JVP.
Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation; her chest is clear.

steps.x: **A. Cardiac tamponade.** Beck's triad on anticoagulation = cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with metastatic lung cancer has a large pericardial effusion and is hypotensive with a pulse rate of 132 bpm and BP 84/60 mmHg. He is drowsy. The doctor watches his neck veins with the patient sitting at 45° while he breathes in and out.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the JVP?
o: Prominent x and y descents with normal height
questions.e: In tamponade the JVP may paradoxically rise on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign), with marked tachycardia and altered mental state.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Large effusion + hypotension + confusion = tamponade. The JVP sign is **Kussmaul's**: it **rises** on inspiration.

elim: Cannon a waves are complete heart block.
Giant v waves are tricuspid regurgitation.
A normal-height JVP does not fit tamponade.
A normal JVP falls on inspiration; that is not abnormal.

steps.x: **E. The JVP rises on inspiration.** Kussmaul's sign: JVP rises with inspiration.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a malignant pericardial effusion. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 88/62 mmHg, and her JVP is raised at 9 cm. A manual BP shows the systolic pressure falls by 22 mmHg when she breathes in. Her JVP waveform is examined carefully.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the JVP waveform?
questions.e: Tamponade causes pulsus paradoxus (systolic fall over 15 mmHg on inspiration) and loss of the y descent, because the compressed ventricle cannot fill rapidly in early diastole.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: falls by 22 mmHg when she breathes in
steps.x: A **>15 mmHg** inspiratory fall = **pulsus paradoxus** = tamponade, which **abolishes the y descent**.

elim: Cannon a waves are complete heart block.
Giant v waves are tricuspid regurgitation.
Large a waves are pulmonary hypertension or tricuspid stenosis.
A prominent, steep y descent is constrictive pericarditis, not tamponade.

steps.x: **A. Absent y descent.** Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus and an absent y descent.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man had coronary bypass surgery 4 years ago. He has 1 year of ankle swelling, abdominal distension and tiredness. His JVP is raised at 8 cm and rises further with pressure on the abdomen. He has shifting dullness. Chest X-ray shows a normal-sized heart with pericardial calcification.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap
questions.e: Constrictive pericarditis gives an early diastolic pericardial knock as filling stops abruptly against the rigid pericardium, with right heart failure signs and positive hepatojugular reflux.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: rises further with pressure on the abdomen
steps.x: Previous surgery + right-sided failure + **calcified** pericardium + normal heart size = **constriction**: listen for the **knock**.

elim: S4 needs a stiff ventricle, not a constricting pericardium.
An opening snap is mitral stenosis.
A pansystolic apical murmur is mitral regurgitation.
Fixed split S2 is an atrial septal defect.

steps.x: **A. Early diastolic pericardial knock.** Constrictive pericarditis: early diastolic pericardial knock.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman had a large anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago, complicated 3 weeks later by fever and pericardial pain. She now has 6 months of increasing abdominal swelling and leg oedema. Her JVP is raised at 7 cm with positive hepatojugular reflux. Echocardiography shows a thickened pericardium with normal left ventricular function.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.e: Dressler's syndrome weeks after MI can lead to constrictive pericarditis: a thickened rigid pericardium limits filling, causing right heart failure with normal LV function.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: complicated 3 weeks later by fever and pericardial pain
thickened pericardium with normal left ventricular function
steps.x: Past **Dressler's** + right heart failure + **thickened pericardium** with good LV = constriction.

elim: Cirrhosis causes ascites with a low or normal JVP.
Tamponade is acute with hypotension.
Her LV function is normal.
TR gives a pansystolic murmur and giant v waves; echo shows the pericardium is the problem.

steps.x: **C. Constrictive pericarditis.** Dressler's can progress to constrictive pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has 2 days of sharp central chest pain worse on lying down and coughing. He had a viral illness last week. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. ECG shows PR depression and concave ST elevation in most leads. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mildly raised troponin and raised CRP are common in acute pericarditis; the positional pain, viral prodrome and PR depression make it the diagnosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: worse on lying down and coughing
PR depression and concave ST elevation in most leads
steps.x: Positional pain + viral illness + **PR depression**. A small troponin rise does not make it an MI.

elim: Dissection gives tearing pain to the back.
Pneumonia gives productive cough and consolidation, not widespread ST elevation.
NSTEMI does not cause PR depression or widespread concave ST elevation.
PE gives hypoxia and tachycardia, not these ECG changes.

steps.x: **A. Acute pericarditis.** Pericarditis can mildly raise troponin; CRP is raised.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has 6 months of fatigue, joint pains with swollen fingers, a photosensitive facial rash and painless mouth ulcers. Over 2 days she has become breathless and light-headed. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 82/58 mmHg and JVP raised at 8 cm. Her heart sounds are muffled.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: SLE (arthralgia, synovitis, malar rash, oral ulcers) is a risk factor for pericardial effusion and tamponade; Beck's triad is present.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Features of **SLE** plus **Beck's triad** = tamponade.

elim: Acute pericarditis alone does not cause hypotension with raised JVP and muffled sounds.
Constriction is chronic, over months.
Libman-Sacks vegetations cause murmurs and emboli, not Beck's triad.
PE can cause hypotension and raised JVP but not muffled heart sounds.

steps.x: **B. Cardiac tamponade.** SLE + Beck's triad = cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has acute pericarditis after a viral illness. He is haemodynamically stable. His 12-lead ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression. The registrar points to a further sign in lead II between the end of the T wave and the next P wave.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on the ECG?
questions.e: Spodick's sign, a downsloping TP segment, is a recognised ECG feature of acute pericarditis alongside PR depression and saddle-shaped ST elevation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: acute pericarditis after a viral illness
between the end of the T wave and the next P wave
steps.x: The segment from **T to P** in pericarditis slopes down: **Spodick's sign**.

elim: Delta waves are Wolff-Parkinson-White.
J waves are hypothermia.
Q waves suggest established infarction.
U waves are hypokalaemia.

steps.x: **B. Downsloping TP segment.** Pericarditis ECG: PR depression, saddle ST elevation, Spodick's sign.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has acute pericarditis diagnosed on her symptoms and a 12-lead ECG showing PR depression. She is comfortable after analgesia. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and JVP is not raised. Her heart sounds are normal.
questions.q: Which further investigation should be performed in all such patients?
questions.e: All patients with suspected acute pericarditis should have a transthoracic echo to look for an effusion.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Even a stable patient needs a **TTE** to look for an **effusion**.

elim: Catheterisation is invasive and not indicated.
CT coronary angiography looks for coronary disease.
An exercise test is for angina.
Biopsy is reserved for unexplained chronic cases.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiography.** All suspected acute pericarditis: TTE.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with hypothyroidism has 6 weeks of gradually worsening breathlessness and chest heaviness. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg and she has no pulsus paradoxus. Her JVP is raised at 5 cm and heart sounds are quiet. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosing a pericardial effusion and assessing for tamponade.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Progressive breathlessness, raised JVP, **muffled sounds**, low voltages = effusion; confirm with **echo**.

elim: Cardiac MRI is not first-line for an effusion.
A chest X-ray suggests it but cannot confirm or assess tamponade.
CTPA looks for PE.
Troponin does not show fluid.

steps.x: **D. Echocardiography.** Effusion or tamponade: echocardiography is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with metastatic oesophageal cancer has 3 weeks of breathlessness. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 102/70 mmHg. Echocardiography shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with the heart moving freely within it. A 12-lead ECG is recorded.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
o: Small QRS complexes alternating in height
ST elevation in V1 to V4 only
questions.e: A large effusion causes small QRS complexes with electrical alternans, because the heart swings within the fluid and its axis changes from beat to beat.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Fluid damps the voltage (**small QRS**) and the **swinging** heart changes axis each beat (**electrical alternans**).

elim: Delta waves are pre-excitation.
Peaked T waves are hyperkalaemia.
Flutter waves are atrial flutter.
Regional ST elevation is an anterior STEMI.

steps.x: **D. Small QRS complexes alternating in height.** Large effusion ECG: low voltage + electrical alternans.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with end-stage renal failure has 3 weeks of increasing breathlessness. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. He has a raised JVP and muffled heart sounds but no pulsus paradoxus. His lung fields sound clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: A pericardial effusion enlarges the cardiac silhouette into a globular water-bottle shape, often with clear lungs.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: raised JVP and muffled heart sounds
steps.x: Muffled sounds with a raised JVP = **effusion**; on X-ray the heart looks like a **water bottle**.

elim: Hilar lymphadenopathy suggests sarcoid or lymphoma.
Upper zone fibrosis is TB or sarcoid.
Free air is a perforated viscus.
Lobar collapse does not explain muffled heart sounds.

steps.x: **C. Enlarged globular cardiac silhouette.** Effusion CXR: water bottle heart.

questions.stem: A 26 year old rugby player has acute viral pericarditis confirmed on ECG and echocardiography, with no effusion. He has no past medical history, no peptic ulcer disease and no kidney disease. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. He wants to play this weekend.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Naproxen and colchicine with rest from sport
questions.e: First-line treatment for acute pericarditis is an NSAID such as ibuprofen or naproxen plus colchicine, with rest.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
First line: **NSAID + colchicine**, and **rest** (no sport for now).

elim: Antiplatelets are for coronary disease.
Steroids are not first line and increase recurrence.
Paracetamol alone is inadequate and he must rest.
There is no effusion to drain.

steps.x: **B. Naproxen and colchicine with rest from sport.** Acute pericarditis: NSAID + colchicine + rest.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has acute pericarditis after a viral illness. Eight months ago he had a perforated gastric ulcer that needed surgery. He is haemodynamically stable and echocardiography shows no effusion. His eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: NSAIDs are avoided in peptic ulcer disease, so colchicine monotherapy is the second-line choice.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Peptic ulcer history: **avoid NSAIDs**, use **colchicine alone**.

elim: Ibuprofen is an NSAID; he has had a perforated ulcer.
Naproxen is an NSAID.
Antibiotics do not treat viral pericarditis.
Pericardiectomy is for constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: **A. Colchicine monotherapy.** NSAID contraindicated: colchicine monotherapy.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has cardiac tamponade with BP 76/50 mmHg. Ultrasound is not immediately available and the registrar must perform a blind emergency pericardiocentesis using the sub-xiphoid approach. A student asks where the needle goes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate needle position and direction?
o: Just left of the xiphoid, aimed toward the left shoulder
Just right of the xiphoid, aimed toward the right hip
Through the sternum at the level of the nipples
questions.e: The sub-xiphoid needle goes in just left of the xiphoid, aimed toward the left shoulder; this route is preferred for blind drainage because it carries a lower pneumothorax risk.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Sub-xiphoid: **just left of the xiphoid**, aim to the **left shoulder**, away from the pleura.

elim: The fifth intercostal space in the mid-axillary line is for chest drains.
Aiming right and down misses the heart and risks the liver.
The second intercostal space is for decompressing a tension pneumothorax.
The sternum is not a pericardiocentesis route.

steps.x: **B. Just left of the xiphoid, aimed toward the left shoulder.** Pericardiocentesis: left of the xiphoid toward the left shoulder.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has 5 days of fever and chest pain. He has a pericardial friction rub. Today he is drowsy. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 134 bpm, BP 78/50 mmHg and JVP raised at 9 cm. His heart sounds are muffled. Bedside echo shows a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Fever with a rub plus hypotension, raised JVP and muffled sounds means tamponade, needing urgent drainage by pericardiocentesis (ultrasound guided, sub-xiphoid).

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Fever + rub + **Beck's triad** + RV collapse = tamponade: **drain now**.

elim: NSAIDs and colchicine treat pericarditis but will not relieve tamponade.
Diuretics reduce preload and worsen tamponade.
Waiting 24 hours risks cardiac arrest.
Oral antibiotics do not relieve compression.

steps.x: **E. Urgent pericardiocentesis.** Tamponade: urgent pericardiocentesis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with metastatic melanoma has had two pericardiocenteses for malignant tamponade in the past 6 weeks. The effusion has reaccumulated and she is breathless with BP 94/66 mmHg. She is not fit for open surgery. Her oncologist is still offering systemic treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Recurrent neoplastic tamponade, such as from melanoma, can be managed by percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy, which creates a window for fluid to drain.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Malignant**, **recurrent** effusion, unfit for surgery: **balloon pericardiotomy**.

elim: Colchicine does not prevent malignant reaccumulation.
NSAIDs and colchicine treat inflammatory pericarditis, not malignant effusion.
Diuretics worsen tamponade.
Pericardiectomy is open surgery for constriction; she is unfit.

steps.x: **D. Percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy.** Neoplastic tamponade: percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with stage 5 chronic kidney disease, not yet on dialysis, has 3 days of chest pain eased sitting forward and a pericardial friction rub. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. Echocardiography shows a small effusion with no tamponade. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Uraemic pericarditis in CKD is treated by removing the urea with urgent haemodialysis.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: stage 5 chronic kidney disease, not yet on dialysis
steps.x: The cause is **uraemia**, so treat the cause: **dialysis**.

elim: NSAIDs are avoided in advanced CKD.
Steroids do not treat uraemic pericarditis.
Pericardiectomy is for constriction.
There is no tamponade to drain.

steps.x: **D. Urgent haemodialysis.** Uraemic pericarditis: urgent haemodialysis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman had viral pericarditis 2 weeks ago and is improving on ibuprofen and colchicine. She has no breathlessness. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and JVP not raised. Echocardiography shows a small 6 mm pericardial effusion with no chamber collapse.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the effusion?
questions.e: Small effusions are monitored; pericardiocentesis is for symptomatic or large effusions or tamponade.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Small**, asymptomatic, no collapse: **watch** it.

elim: Balloon pericardiotomy is for recurrent malignant effusions.
Pericardiectomy is for constrictive pericarditis.
A window is for recurrent large effusions.
Drainage is for symptomatic effusion or tamponade.

steps.x: **A. Monitor with repeat echocardiography.** Small effusion: monitor. Symptomatic: pericardiocentesis.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has confirmed constrictive pericarditis with a thickened, calcified pericardium. Despite furosemide and spironolactone he still has severe ascites, leg oedema and breathlessness on minimal exertion. He is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Constrictive pericarditis is managed with diuretics, and surgical pericardiectomy when symptoms persist.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Diuretics have failed; the rigid shell must be **removed**: **pericardiectomy**.

elim: Colchicine treats acute inflammation, not a calcified shell.
Transplant is not needed; the myocardium is normal.
Balloon pericardiotomy drains malignant fluid; there is no effusion.
There is no fluid to drain in constriction.

steps.x: **D. Pericardiectomy.** Constriction: diuretics, then pericardiectomy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has acute viral pericarditis. Her chest pain is sharp, worse when she breathes in or lies flat and much better when she sits up and leans forward. Echocardiography shows a thin rim of pericardial fluid.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pain?
o: Inflamed pericardial layers irritating pain fibres
questions.e: The pericardium is a fibrous sac with visceral and parietal layers separated by fluid; inflammation increases fluid and irritates pain fibres, giving positional, pleuritic pain.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: sharp, worse when she breathes in or lies flat
steps.x: Inflamed **pericardial layers** rub and stimulate **pain fibres**; leaning forward eases the contact.

elim: Coronary spasm gives angina-like pain at rest, not positional pain.
Ischaemic pain is not positional or pleuritic.
Oesophageal spasm gives swallowing-related pain.
Pulmonary infarction gives pleuritic pain with hypoxia, not eased leaning forward.

steps.x: **B. Inflamed pericardial layers irritating pain fibres.** Pericarditis pain: inflamed pericardium irritating pain fibres; positional and pleuritic.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is 4 hours after cardiac surgery. His chest drain output stops suddenly, and he becomes hypotensive with BP 74/48 mmHg, a raised JVP and a falling cardiac output. Echocardiography shows a clot compressing the right atrium and right ventricle.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypotension?
o: Loss of vascular tone from sepsis
Pericardial pressure exceeding chamber pressure, impairing filling
questions.e: Tamponade occurs when intrapericardial pressure equals or exceeds the pressure in the cardiac chambers, so the heart cannot fill and cardiac output falls.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: clot compressing the right atrium and right ventricle
steps.x: The blocked drain lets blood collect; once pericardial pressure **exceeds chamber pressure** the heart **cannot fill**.

elim: LVOT obstruction is a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy feature, not this picture.
Sepsis gives a low JVP and warm peripheries.
PE does not cause clot compressing the heart on echo.
Stunning reduces contraction but the echo shows external compression.

steps.x: **E. Pericardial pressure exceeding chamber pressure, impairing filling.** Tamponade: pericardial pressure exceeds chamber pressure, filling fails.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man had tuberculous pericarditis 5 years ago. He now has slowly progressive ankle swelling and ascites. Echocardiography shows normal systolic function, a thickened calcified pericardium and abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole.
questions.q: Which best explains his symptoms?
o: A rigid fibrotic pericardium limits diastolic filling
Acute fluid accumulation raises intrapericardial pressure
Infiltration of the myocardium by amyloid
questions.e: Chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis and calcification, forming a rigid shell that limits filling, like tamponade but over a longer timescale.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.
Past inflammation leaves a **rigid shell**; filling stops abruptly when the heart hits it, **chronically**.

elim: Acute fluid pressure is tamponade, which is sudden.
His systolic function is normal.
Amyloid thickens the myocardium, not the pericardium.
